questions.question: Separate the three economic systems by who answers the three questions, justify South Africa's double label, and bind each factor of production to its reward with profit argued as the residual.
questions.expected_answer: Every economy answers what, how and for whom. Free market: prices answer — purchases signal wants, profit pulls resources, the state stays out; efficient and inventive but unequal, with public goods unbuilt and externalities unpriced. Centrally planned: officials answer — outputs and prices fixed from above; fair on paper but blind without price signals, so gluts sit beside shortages and innovation stalls. Mixed: markets allocate while the state taxes, regulates and provides — every real economy. South Africa is mixed AND dualistic: a first-world financial and industrial economy operating alongside a vast informal and subsistence economy. Factors and rewards: natural resources earn rent; labour earns wages, upgraded by education and health into human capital; capital — produced means of production, not money itself — earns interest; entrepreneurship earns profit, the residual left after rent, wages and interest are settled, which can be zero or negative — profit is the price of bearing the risk.

questions.question: Explain how the production, income and expenditure methods reconcile to one GDP, classify each expenditure component precisely, and argue infrastructure as both engine and gate using a South African case.
questions.expected_answer: Production: sum value added by every industry (gross value added), add product taxes, subtract subsidies — GDP at market prices. Income: sum the factor rewards — wages plus rent plus interest plus profit. Expenditure: C plus I plus G plus X minus M. All three measure the same flow, so they must land on one figure. Components: C is household consumption, the largest block; G is government consumption — nurses', teachers' and police salaries, never grant transfers; I is gross fixed capital formation — plants, roads, machines that build future capacity; X minus M corrects for the border because imports meet demand without local production; GNI adds residents' foreign earnings and subtracts foreigners' local earnings. Infrastructure: as engine, every sector hangs on power, transport, water and communications — the load-shedding years interrupted production, bankrupted small firms and priced away investors; as gate, the household with power, water, transport and signal can work, study and trade, while the household without them is locked out of the economy.

questions.question: Using the chips, the taxi fare and the vetkoek stall, diagnose elasticity in each case, predict the till, and state and verify the profit-maximising rule for a price taker.
questions.expected_answer: Chips with rival brands: elastic — substitutes let buyers bounce away, so the percentage quantity change exceeds the percentage price change (above one); raising the price shrinks total revenue, and a price cut can fill the till instead. Taxi fare: inelastic — a necessity with no substitute takes a small budget share, so riders still ride (below one); raising the fare swells revenue because the few lost riders are outweighed by the higher fare on those who stay. Vetkoek stall: a price taker sells every unit at the going fifteen rand, so marginal revenue equals price; keep frying while the next vetkoek costs less than fifteen rand and stop the moment its marginal cost passes fifteen — produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Verify in a table by comparing the MR and MC columns row by row, and state profit as total revenue minus total cost at that output; fixed costs like the stand fee are owed even at zero output and do not enter the next-unit decision.
